title: Indian Envoy Meets Distressed Women Workers in Oman, Pledges Quick Action
excerpt: Ambassador Prashant Pise visited Indian women at the embassy's shelter in Muscat, hearing their complaints of abuse, wage theft and abandonment by employers.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Ambassador Prashant Pise met distressed Indian women workers in Oman, addressing their grievances.
  • Women reported abuse, wage theft, and abandonment by employers, prompting embassy intervention.
  • The case of Shabnam Begum highlights systemic issues faced by Indian domestic workers in the Gulf.
  • India's labor agreements with Gulf countries do not specifically protect domestic workers.
  • Approximately 700,000 Indians live in Oman, with 6% being women in vulnerable domestic roles.

Indian Embassy in Muscat
  • India's Ambassador to Oman, Prashant Pise, met distressed Indian women domestic workers at the embassy shelter in Muscat on Monday.
  • The embassy said it heard the women's grievances — including abuse, wage theft and abandonment — and assured them of prompt resolution through its Community Affairs team.
  • The outreach follows the case of Hyderabad resident Shabnam Begum, who alleged she was forced to work 12–15 hours a day without pay before escaping to the embassy.
  • India has labour agreements with all six Gulf countries, but these frameworks do not specifically cover domestic workers, leaving them vulnerable to exploitation.

India's Ambassador to Oman, Prashant Pise, met a group of distressed Indian women working as domestic workers in the Gulf country and assured them that their complaints would be addressed swiftly, the Indian Embassy in Muscat said on Monday.

Pise visited the women at a shelter run by the Indian mission, where free boarding and lodging are provided to workers in distress, according to a statement shared by the embassy on X. The ambassador met women "who have left their employers' households or have been abandoned by their employers," the post said.

https://x.com/BradPorcellato/status/2079144649986343024

"Their grievances and complaints were heard, while assuring them prompt action by the Embassy's Community Affairs team to reach an early resolution."

— Indian Embassy in Muscat, statement on X

The Shabnam Begum Case

The ambassador's outreach comes against the backdrop of a case that drew fresh attention to the plight of Indian domestic workers in the Gulf. Shabnam Begum, a Hyderabad resident, alleged that she was taken to Muscat with the promise of a better-paying domestic job but was instead made to work 12 to 15 hours a day across multiple households without wages. She also alleged that she was assaulted, denied adequate food and had her mobile phone confiscated before she managed to escape and take shelter at the Indian Embassy.

The mission said on Saturday that it had taken cognisance of Shabnam Begum's case and was pursuing it "at the appropriate levels," according to India Today, which cited PTI inputs.

A Recurring Pattern Across the Gulf

The episode is far from isolated. Indian women recruited for domestic work in Gulf countries have repeatedly reported being lured by unscrupulous agents, only to face passport confiscation, forced labour, physical abuse and wage theft upon arrival. In 2025, Sajida Begum from Hyderabad's Kalapathar area was similarly trapped in Muscat after being promised a housemaid's job, only to be coerced into working 16-hour days and denied contact with her family. Her daughter appealed directly to the Ministry of External Affairs for help.

In October 2025, Union Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal intervened after 36 Indian workers in Oman were found living in distressing conditions, subjected to delayed wages, cramped accommodation and passport confiscation. The workers were sheltered at a local gurdwara and repatriated.

Legal Gaps in Worker Protections
›Labour agreements exclude domestic workers.
›Oman's labor law does not protect domestic workers.
›Kafala system ties visas to employers, limiting mobility.
›Human Rights Watch reports risks of deportation for fleeing workers.

Structural Gaps in Protections

India has labour and manpower cooperation agreements with all six Gulf Cooperation Council countries — Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE. These provide a framework for addressing issues related to the welfare and protection of Indian workers through regular bilateral consultations. However, the agreements do not specifically mention domestic workers, according to the Indian Council of World Affairs, leaving a significant gap in the legal safety net for a highly vulnerable workforce.

Oman's labour law excludes domestic workers from its protections, and the country's kafala (sponsorship) system ties workers' visas to their employers, making it difficult for them to change jobs or leave abusive situations without risking arrest for "absconding." A Human Rights Watch report has documented how workers who flee abuse can face deportation, fines and even criminal complaints filed by their former employers.

India's e-Migrate system, introduced in 2015, requires employers in nearly 20 countries to obtain online clearance before hiring Indian blue-collar workers and domestic help. The embassy in Muscat also maintains a shelter for distressed workers and has periodically blacklisted recruitment agencies found to be abusive.

What Lies Ahead

Pise's visit to the shelter signals an early priority for the new envoy, who assumed charge on June 14 after previously serving as Additional Secretary in the Ministry of External Affairs handling emigration policy and migration-related matters. The embassy's latest outreach underlined both the support being extended to distressed Indian domestic workers in Oman and the continuing concerns over their safety, working conditions and unpaid wages.

With an estimated 700,000 Indians living and working in Oman — roughly 6 percent of them women — migrant rights advocates say systemic reforms, not just case-by-case interventions, are needed to protect those most at risk.
